sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The prospective, observational IDEAL study evaluated the effectiveness and safety of the long-acting fluocinolone acetonide (FAc) implant in patients with chronic diabetic macular edema (DME) and examined the influence of various baseline factors on treatment success.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Patients with persistent DME despite prior treatment with available therapies who received FAc implant were included from 35 ophthalmological centers in Germany and monitored for up to 24 months. Demographic and clinical data, including disease duration, previous treatment, best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), central macular thickness (CMT), intraocular pressure (IOP), and adverse events were recorded at routine visits and analyzed descriptively, also in predefined groups.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Overall, 214 eyes from 185 patients (57% male) with a mean (SD) age of 66.2 (9.7) years were followed up for a mean (SD) of 21.53 (6.49) months. Functional and anatomical improvements occurred rapidly within 1 week after FAc injection and were sustained over 24 months in these previously intensively treated eyes (72.9% laser treatment, 79.9% intravitreal therapy with dexamethasone and/or anti-VEGF inhibitors, 28.9% vitrectomy). Mean BCVA increased from 55.8 (18.4) letters at baseline to 60.9 (19.0) letters at 24 months, with comparable results across subgroups defined by baseline characteristics. Eyes with fewer than two prior dexamethasone injections showed a more pronounced CMT reduction. In a subset with early follow-up, greater CMT reduction at week 1 was strongly associated with greater CMT reduction at month 1. Mean IOP in the total cohort increased from 15.3 ± 3.3 mm Hg to 17.4 ± 4.8 mm Hg within 9 months and returned to 16.7 ± 5.0 by month 24. IOP lowering was required in 35.5% of eyes (topical medication), and 4.6% underwent IOP-lowering surgery.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The IDEAL observational study demonstrated a rapid onset of effect and reaffirmed the long-term efficacy and safety of the FAc implant in a large cohort of patients with persistent DME despite extensive prior treatment, thus underlining the high medical need of this treatment option for DME patients insufficiently responding to other therapies.
Keywords: Diabetic macular edema, Persistent diabetic macular edema, Intravitreal fluocinolone acetonide

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Diabetic macular edema (DME) is one of the most prevalent microvascular complications among patients with diabetes mellitus, and it remains a leading cause of significant visual impairment and blindness [1]. Globally, approximately 5.5% of individuals with diabetes mellitus are affected by DME [1], and as diabetes incidence continues to rise, the number of DME patients is expected to increase by 2045 [2, 3].

Currently, the standard first-line treatment for visual impairment caused by center-involved DME consists of intravitreal injections of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF). Corticosteroids also remain a key treatment for chronic persistent DME [4, 5]. However, managing DME and preserving long-term vision preservation can be challenging in clinical practice for several reasons. Many patients present with a complex medical history due to their underlying diabetes and additional comorbidities. Furthermore, many individuals with DME have undergone multiple treatments over extended periods. Adherence, a crucial factor in treatment success, is often a challenge in diabetes care, where patients are burdened by numerous appointments and medications [6]. Undertreatment is a major issue with anti-VEGF therapy for DME in real life settings [7]. According to data from the IRIS® (Intelligent Research in Sight) registry, 52% of patients with DME discontinued anti-VEGF treatment after an average of 6 months in clinical practice [8]. Although about one-third of the patients reinitiated therapy, interruptions in treatment contribute to long-term decline in visual acuity and an increased risk of disease progression in DME patients [9].

Additionally, depending on the drug used, about 30–65% of patients with DME exhibit an inadequate response to anti-VEGF treatment, experiencing persistent and recurrent retinal fluid [10]. Even with the recently introduced anti-VEGF agents, a certain proportion of patients still have intraretinal fluid [11–13]. One key factor contributing to this limited response is the multifactorial and complex pathophysiology of macular edema, where the inflammatory component is often more pronounced and prolonged than the VEGF component [14–16]. Recent research emphasizes the critical role of inflammation in DME’s complex pathophysiology, positioning it as an important therapeutic target [16, 17]. Elevated levels of inflammatory molecules have been detected in ocular fluids from DME eyes, and a correlation has been observed between their concentration and retinal thickness on optical coherence tomography (OCT) has been reported [16, 18]. Additionally, eyes with DME that do not respond adequately to VEGF inhibitors have shown higher levels of these inflammatory molecules [18].

Unlike anti-VEGF therapy, which primarily targets VEGF levels, corticosteroids provide a broad range of anti-inflammatory actions and serve as a secondary valuable treatment option for managing macular edema [16]. The long-acting fluocinolone acetonide implant (FAc implant; ILUVIEN®, Alimera Sciences, Inc., Dublin, Ireland) is approved for the treatment of vision impairment associated with chronic DME, considered insufficiently responsive to available therapies [19]. The implant is administered into the vitreous, where it continuously releases a microdose of FAc (0.2 μg/day FAc) for up to 36 months. The safety and efficacy of the FAc implant were demonstrated in the FAME randomized controlled trials and have been supported by several real-world studies across diverse patient populations [20–23].

The IDEAL prospective study aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of the FAc implant in a real-world setting for treating visual impairment due to DME that has not sufficiently responded to available therapies. Additionally, the study sought to examine how baseline visual acuity, DME duration, and prior intravitreal corticosteroid injection influence the success of FAc implant treatment.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The open-label, noncontrolled, multicenter, single-arm cohort study IDEAL (ILUVIEN Implant for chronic DiabEtic MAcuLar edema) was conducted at ophthalmological centers in Germany and Austria. Patients were examined between April 2016 and September 2022. The follow-up period was 24 months. Adult patients (aged 18 years or older) who were treated with FAc implant for visual impairment were included due to persistent DME despite treatment with available therapies, according to the summary of product characteristics. The decision for treatment with the FAc implant was made prior to enrollment and was independent of participation in the trial. Key exclusion criteria were contraindications according to the ILUVIEN® summary of product characteristics, e.g., preexisting glaucoma, active or suspected infection of the eye or periocular region, or hypersensitivity to any of the device components. All patients provided written informed consent for participation in this study. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Germany’s Data Protection Act (AMG §4 (23), Satz 3). Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of the University Hospital of Tübingen (024/2016BO2; February 25, 2016).

At baseline, demographic data as well as information on diabetes mellitus and the history of DME, other concomitant diseases and medication, as well as lens status and stage of diabetic retinopathy (using fluorescein angiography) in the treatment eye were recorded. Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) measured with Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) charts, intraocular pressure (IOP), and central macular thickness (CMT) in OCT were assessed at baseline, week 1, and approximately at 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24 months following FAc injection in accordance with clinical routine. CMT was measured using Topcon 3D OCT-2000, Heidelberg Spectralis, and Carl Zeiss Cirrus. Moreover, supplemental ocular treatments administered, cataract formation, and incidence of IOP elevation (IOP change of >10 mm Hg from baseline and an increase >30 mm Hg) and management (use of IOP-lowering medication to control IOP) were documented. Adverse events were documented throughout the study.

The analyses were descriptive. Missing values were not replaced. Data processing and statistical analysis were carried out using the SAS® version 9.4 program. Data were reported as mean ± standard deviation (SD), 95% confidence intervals (CI), or relative frequencies unless otherwise stated. A linear mixed effects model was employed to analyze repeated measurements over time. The model included fixed effects for the categorical factors under study, as well as their interaction, to evaluate both main effects and potential differential temporal patterns. Because multiple observations were recorded for each individual, a repeated-measures structure was specified to account for within-subject correlation. For the analysis of onset of effect and the predictive value of early anatomical response, eyes with complete CMT data at baseline, week 1, month 1, and month 24 were included (n = 65). Mean changes in CMT were calculated for each visit. Consistency of CMT measurements across time points was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). The association between early CMT change and subsequent anatomical outcomes was examined using linear regression models with change in CMT at month 1 or month 24 as the dependent variable and the CMT change at week 1 as the main independent variable; multivariable models were additionally adjusted for baseline CMT. To further characterize response patterns, patients were stratified into tertiles according to the magnitude of their week 1 CMT reduction, and longitudinal CMT trajectories were compared between these tertile groups.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In total, 214 eyes from 185 patients were included in the study. The mean observation period was 21.53 ± 6.49 months. Table 1 summarizes demographics, baseline characteristics, and prior treatments. The mean age was 66.2 ± 9.7 years, and the majority of patients was reported to have type 2 diabetes (92%) with a mean time from diagnosis of 16.9 ± 11.4 years and additional systemic comorbidities (75%). The mean time since initial diagnosis of DME was 3.9 ± 2.9 years. Within the last 12 months before FAc injection, the majority of study eyes had been treated for DME: 72.9% had received focal laser therapy, 79.9% had received intravitreal therapy (predominantly dexamethasone [64.5%], ranibizumab [44.9%], bevacizumab [24.8%], or aflibercept [25.7%]), and 28.9% had undergone a vitrectomy). Moreover, 72.6% of eyes were pseudophakic, 25.2% had macular ischemia, and 20.6% had other ocular diseases.

sec.title: Rationale for Treatment with the FAc Implant and Use of Adjunctive Therapy
sec.p: Most common reasons for initiating treatment with the FAc implant were “insufficient effect of previous therapy” (88.8%), “pronounced edema” (55.6%), and “high number of recurrences during pretreatment” (46.7%). Adjunctive therapy to FAc implant was recorded as part of the routine treatment patterns following FAc implantation and was considered to be required in 31.3% of eyes during the 24 months period. Of these, 22% (n = 48/214) received concomitant intravitreal anti-VEGF, 6.5% (14/214) received intravitreal dexamethasone, and 2.8% (6/214) a second FAc implant. Conversely, 68.7% of eyes did not require any additional intravitreal therapy for DME for up to 24 months after FAc implantation.

sec.title: Functional Outcomes
sec.p: In the overall population, BCVA stabilized with a moderate improvement following FAc injection across the entire 24-month observation period. The mean (±SD) BCVA increased from 55.8 ± 18.4 letters at baseline to 60.9 ± 19.0 at the end of the study. While the subgroup of eyes with a lower baseline vision (<65 letters, n = 119) experienced distinct gains in mean BCVA, eyes with a higher baseline vision of ≥65 letters (n = 92) showed minimal losses with vision maintained over the 24 months follow-up period (shown in Fig. 1). In addition, analyses of BCVA by the baseline characteristics “DME duration,” “dexamethasone pretreatment,” and “previous vitrectomy” demonstrate comparable and stable visual acuity outcomes across all subgroups over the 24-month period (Table 2).

sec.title: Anatomical Outcomes
sec.p: Following FAc injection, a rapid and significant decrease in CMT was observed in the total population, which subsequently remained stable during the follow-up until month 24 (p = 0.001) (shown in Fig. 2). In line with the visual acuity results, the analyses of CMT by baseline factors “DME duration” and “previous vitrectomy” also demonstrated a comparable rapid and sustained CMT reduction up to month 24 in these subgroups (Table 3). In all subgroups CMT decreased significantly during the study compared to baseline (p < 0.001), with no significant differences between subgroups. With respect to the baseline factor “Dexamethasone pretreatment,” the CMT reduction was significantly greater in the subgroup with fewer dexamethasone injections (p = 0.005) (shown in Fig. 3).

sec.title: Onset of Effect
sec.p: A more detailed analysis of the initial period following FAc injection reveals a rapid onset of the treatment effect. For patients with available BCVA data at all time points (n = 82), a mean improvement was observed from week 1 onward, which was statistically significant at month 1 and at month 24 (Fig. 4a). CMT data were available for all time points for 65 study participants. At the first week, mean CMT demonstrates significant improvement, with mean CMT continuing to show further improvement at month 1 and month 24 for the study cohort (as shown in Fig. 4a). The global ICC (CI of 0.557 [0.428–0.689]) indicated a good consistency between the different timepoints. The pairwise ICC showed the highest agreement between week 1 and month 1 (0.909 [0.860–0.944]), when compared to the larger time spans (week 1 to month 24: 0.294 [0.053–0.504]; month 1 to month 24: 0.466 [0.243–0.647]) (Fig. 4b).

Early response shows a close association with the decrease in retinal thickness after 1 month and—somewhat less strongly—with thickness after 24 months.

sec.p: A greater reduction in CMT at week 1 was strongly and significantly associated with a greater reduction at month 1 (β = 0.999 µm/µm; CI: 0.861–0.114; p < 0.0001; R2 = 0.758). A greater reduction in CMT at week 1 was significantly associated with a greater reduction at 24 months (β = 0.988 µm/µm; CI: 0.606–1.370; p = 0.0001; R2 = 0.290).

In the multivariable model adjusting for baseline CMT, the response at week 1 remained a strong independent predictor of the reduction at month 1 (β = 0.944 µm/µm; CI: 0.781–1.108; p < 0.0001). Baseline CMT was also independently associated with greater improvement (β = −0.07 µm/µm; p = 0.203). The model explained 76.9% of the variance in month 1 CMT change. For the 24-month outcome, the association between week 1 change and long-term CMT reduction was no longer significantly after adjusting for baseline (β = 0.420 µm/µm; CI −0.050 to 0.780; p = 0.026), whereas baseline CMT emerged as a strong independent predictor of long-term improvement (β = −0.720 µm/µm; CI −0.960 to −0.480; p < 0.0001). The adjusted 24-month model demonstrated substantially greater explanatory power (R2 = 0.548), indicating that long-term anatomical outcomes are predominantly driven by baseline CMT rather than the early week 1 response. When patients were sorted into tertiles based on their early response, the tertile with the strongest early response also showed a sustained stronger reduction in CMT at later time points (Fig. 4c).

sec.title: IOP and Cataract-Related Events
sec.p: Mean IOP in the total population increased from 15.3 ± 3.3 mm Hg to 17.4 ± 4.8 mm Hg within 9 months, but then returned to 16.7 ± 5.0 by month 24. An IOP increase of ≥10 mm Hg was documented in 15.4% of eyes (n = 33), while one eye (0.5%) had a reading of >30 mm Hg. After FAc injection, 35.5% of eyes (n = 76) were treated with IOP-lowering medication, while 4.6% of eyes (n = 10) required IOP-lowering surgery. Of those patients who were phakic at baseline (n = 58), cataract surgery was performed in 39 eyes (67.2%) following FAc injection.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The IDEAL observational study includes a large and representative cohort of DME patients from routine clinical practice, reinforcing the high medical need for the FAc implant in those with inadequate response to other therapies. It also highlights the long-term efficacy and safety of the FAc implant in real-world settings.

Even in this patient cohort with severely pretreated eyes, where multiple anti-VEGF and dexamethasone injections had been unsuccessful, FAc injection led to a reduction in macular edema and sustained stabilization of visual acuity over 24 months. Particularly for these high-need subgroups, the FAc implant may serve as an effective long-term treatment option for maintaining visual stability and reducing macular edema.

This study provides a specific analysis of early response to FAc implantation at week 1 in a cohort of extensively pretreated patients with DME in routine clinical practice (Fig. 4). We observed a rapid and sustained treatment effect: within 7 days of injection, both visual acuity and retinal thickness had improved, with visual acuity continuing to increase by month 1 and the reduction in retinal thickness being largely maintained throughout the follow-up period. These findings are in line with the PALADIN study, which also reported statistically significant improvements in central retinal thickness and BCVA as early as day 7 that were preserved at most subsequent visits in a longer-term setting. Our regression analyses further indicate that the magnitude of early CMT reduction at week 1 is a strong independent predictor of short-term anatomical outcome at month 1, whereas long-term CMT change over 24 months appears to be driven predominantly by baseline CMT rather than the early week 1 response. Taken together, these data, along with signals from another observational study in a different DME cohort [22], support the concept that FAc implantation is associated with a rapid onset of action and sustained anatomical control and that early anatomical change may help anticipate short-term treatment response in real-world practice.

When interpreting the results of this study, it is important to consider that the included patients in this study had multiple comorbidities and had been living with diabetes, diabetic retinopathy (DR), and DME for many years. Additionally, their eyes had undergone extensive prior treatment: approximately three-quarters of the eyes had received laser therapy and were pseudophakic, 80% had undergone intravitreal injections (primarily dexamethasone), and nearly one-third had a history of vitrectomy. Despite this extensive pretreatment, the FAc implant improved retinal anatomy and stabilized visual acuity, with all subgroups benefiting similarly.

In line with previous studies, the current findings suggest that timely FAc implantation offers significant benefits [23]; in patients with high baseline visual acuity (≥65 letters), this level of acuity was maintained throughout the entire 24-month follow-up period. Additionally, the subgroup with fewer prior dexamethasone treatments showed greater benefits from the FAc injection, particularly in terms of reducing CMT and restoring retinal anatomy. Thus, early FAc implantation may be advantageous for preserving long-term vision at a high level and minimizing the risk of further vision loss. These results align with the IRISS study, which found that earlier treatment with the FAc implant improved the benefit-risk profile for patients [23].

Moreover, it is noteworthy that following FAc implantation, 70% of eyes received no further DME treatments over the 24-month follow-up. Although additional treatments were administered at the physician’s discretion and were not guided by predefined criteria, this reflects routine clinical practice of the participating centers in the management of DME patients and indicates a considerably lower treatment burden for patients compared to anti-VEGF or dexamethasone injections, which typically require multiple administrations over the course of 2 years [24–27]. Especially for patients with diabetes, who are often already burdened by many medical appointments, this can be a significant relief.

The IOP-related events observed in this study align with the findings of the FAME registration trial and other real-world studies [20–23]. Only a third of eyes experienced an IOP increase after FAc injection and just one eye had an IOP spike exceeding 30 mm Hg. Furthermore, the elevated IOP was well controlled with antiglaucomatous medication. These results suggest that in routine clinical practice, an increase in IOP following FAc injection occurs only in a small number of patients and can be effectively managed with topical medication. However, it remains important to monitor IOP after FAc injections to enable timely intervention if necessary. Additionally, the rate of cataract surgery in this study was lower than in the FAME pivotal studies, which is consistent with the findings from real-world IRISS (64.6%) and PALADIN (62.1%) studies [20, 22, 23].

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: As with all data derived from routine clinical care, this study has certain limitations. Unlike controlled clinical trials, pretreatment, monitoring protocols, assessments, additional treatments, and OCT devices used were not standardized in everyday clinical practice, and there was no control arm. This also prevented the comparison of absolute thickness values across different centers. Owing to the observational design, all treatments administered during the 12 months preceding FAc implant initiation were recorded; however, detailed information on the exact interval between the last prior treatment and the first FAc injection – an aspect that may have influenced treatment response – was unfortunately not available. Additionally, the COVID-19 pandemic occurred during the study period, which may have presented further challenges to patient recruitment and maintaining follow-up visits. Furthermore, as the study was solely conducted in Germany, the findings may not be applicable to other countries. Consequently, when interpreting the findings and translating them into clinical practice, particular caution is warranted against overly broad generalization in view of the potential for bias. Nevertheless, the strengths of this study include its prospective design, the 24-month follow-up, and the inclusion of a patient population with diverse baseline characteristics.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In this large cohort of heavily pretreated patients with chronic DME, the FAc implant demonstrated a rapid onset of treatment effect with sustained reduction in macular edema, stabilization of visual acuity, and minimal IOP-related safety concerns. Consistent with prior studies, the IDEAL study reinforces the favorable benefit-risk profile of FAc injection in patients with chronic DME in clinical practice. These results further highlight the value of the FAc implant as an effective treatment option for chronic DME, especially in high-need subgroups.
